strengths: Introduces a training-free semantic understanding pipeline for 3DGS that avoids per-scene semantic optimization and feature compression, substantially reducing training time and feature storage (Table 1).
Combines 2D mask tracking (SAM/DAM2SAM), probabilistic mask lifting, neutral-point filtering, and VLM-based text distillation into a coherent and practical open-vocabulary framework.

Reports strong quantitative results on LERF object selection (mean 54.3 mIoU) and ScanNet semantic segmentation (e.g., 45.5/47.2/53.7 mIoU), outperforming several training-based point-based and pixel-based baselines.
Ablation studies support the VLM-text feature distillation over single-view/averaged/filtered CLIP image features, with a clear margin (54.3 vs 50.1 mIoU).
Qualitative results show improved boundary sharpness and handling of fine-grained language queries compared with OpenGaussian and Dr.Splat.
weaknesses: Key implementation details are missing: threshold values τ_h, τ_α, and η, the number N of top views, the VLM prompt, and full runtime are not reported, making the method difficult to reproduce and assess for robustness.

The central 'polysemous' claim is not directly validated: no experiment evaluates multi-concept queries or per-point multi-label semantics; standard LERF/ScanNet single-label benchmarks do not demonstrate polysemy.

The efficiency claim is only partially supported: Table 1 reports no training time but omits total semantic adaptation/inference time, VLM API cost/latency, and mask tracking time, so the 'hours to minutes' claim lacks direct evidence.

The SOTA framing on LERF is potentially misleading: the 10.7 mIoU improvement is only over point-based Dr.Splat; the overall previous best (LangSplat, 51.4 mIoU) is only 2.9 mIoU lower, and our method underperforms LangSplat/GOI on ramen and teatime categories.

The neutral-point ablation is weak: entropy filtering alone improves only 53.0 to 53.2 mIoU, and no opacity-only baseline or threshold sensitivity analysis is provided, so the contribution of the entropy component is not convincingly isolated.

Fairness/comparison details are incomplete: it is unclear whether baselines for ScanNet were retrained under the same densification-disabled setting, and reliance on proprietary Gemini 2.5 Pro raises reproducibility concerns.

The method depends on pre-trained 3DGS and external models (SAM, DAM2SAM, VLM, CLIP); 'training-free' applies only to the semantic stage, and 'plug-and-play' is limited by the availability and quality of these components.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized. Figure 1 (training-based vs. matching-based pipeline) and Figure 2 (method overview) communicate the training-free matching paradigm effectively, and the contribution bullets map cleanly onto the method sections.

The core practical contribution is real and well supported by Table 1: a training-free, plug-and-play pipeline that eliminates per-scene feature optimization, reporting ~3MB CLIP feature storage versus ~3GB for prior work and ~8GB peak VRAM versus ~20-28GB. This is a meaningful efficiency gain for deployment.

Results are consistent across two benchmarks: LERF object selection (54.3 mean mIoU, highest among all listed methods, including pixel-based ones) and ScanNet open-vocabulary segmentation (45.5/47.2/53.7 mIoU at 19/15/10 classes), where the margin over InstanceGaussian (40.7/42.5/47.9) is clear and consistent.

The technical components are sensible and individually ablated: transmittance-weighted foreground/background accumulation for probabilistic mask lifting (Eqs. 2-3), entropy-plus-opacity neutral-point filtering (Eq. 4), and VLM-based semantic distillation into a canonical CLIP text representation.

Table 5 is an informative ablation: it isolates the effect of VLM text distillation (50.1 -> 54.3 mIoU) against single-view, averaged, and IoU-filtered CLIP image features, providing concrete evidence that viewpoint-inconsistent image features are a genuine bottleneck for matching-based open-vocabulary 3DGS.

Qualitative comparisons in Figures 4 and 5 illustrate sharper boundaries and fewer spurious matches than OpenGaussian and Dr.Splat, which is consistent with the neutral-point and object-level grouping design.
weaknesses: The headline claim of the paper (polysemy) is never evaluated. The title, abstract, and motivation promise that a point can simultaneously belong to 'desk', 'wooden', and 'furniture', yet every reported experiment (LERF object selection, ScanNet per-class segmentation) uses single-concept queries. There is no multi-concept or overlapping-query experiment, so the assertion that prior methods are 'monosemous' and that matching 'inherently' handles polysemy remains unvalidated. The characterization of contrastive methods as 'one-to-one' semantic assignment is also somewhat of a strawman, since CLIP-derived features are continuous and typically do respond to multiple concepts.

The gain over the strongest baseline is marginal and selectively framed. On LERF, 54.3 vs. LangSplat's 51.4 (pixel-based), and the method loses on 2 of 4 categories (ramen 45.6 vs. 52.6; waldo_kitchen 40.9 vs. 44.5). The abstract's 'outperforming the previous best-performing method by 10.7 mIoU' is computed against the best point-based method (Dr.Splat, 43.6) while pixel-based methods are simultaneously presented as competitors, which overstates the headline result.

Efficiency claims are under-substantiated. Table 1 lists 'Train Time: None' for the proposed method, but the pipeline still requires SAM segmentation, DAM2SAM tracking over the full sequence, periodic re-detection, and N-view VLM calls per object. No wall-clock runtime or per-stage cost breakdown is reported, so the 'hours to mere minutes' claim in the abstract is not directly evidenced. VLM inference per object is itself a per-scene cost, not free.

Reproducibility is weakened by dependence on a proprietary VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro). The paper claims the framework is 'VLM-agnostic' but provides no experiment with an alternative model, and the thresholds tau_h and tau_alpha are described only as 'fixed values' without stating their numeric settings. No code or data release statement is visible.

Evidence for the neutral-point module is thin relative to its emphasis in the contributions. Table 4 shows entropy filtering alone yields only +0.2 mIoU and the full model +1.3 mIoU over the baseline, on a single dataset, with no sensitivity analysis for tau_h/tau_alpha. A component presented as a central novelty is supported by a small effect size with no robustness study.

Related-work positioning is incomplete for the VLM-naming component. Object-centric open-vocabulary 3D pipelines that use VLMs/LLMs to caption and name objects before language-feature matching (e.g., ConceptGraphs-style approaches) are not discussed, nor is the relationship to boundary-aware Gaussian segmentation work (GradiSeg, CoB-GS) beyond a citation. This limits the assessed novelty of the VLM distillation step.

Evaluation breadth and metric alignment are limited. Only two datasets are used; the object-selection metric is a 2D rendering mIoU, which is only an indirect proxy for the point-level 3D understanding the paper claims; the ScanNet evaluation disables 3DGS densification to force correspondence with ground-truth point clouds, which may bias the comparison; and no instance-level, box-level, outdoor, or real-world evaluations are provided.

There is an internal inconsistency between the tables: the 'Averaged Image Mat' baseline in Table 5 scores 39.2 mIoU, far below the 51.4 mIoU reported for LangSplat (which is itself an image-feature-based method) in Table 2. The paper does not reconcile how its own image-feature baselines relate to the published baselines it compares against, making the ablation's implications for prior work unclear.

strengths: Genuine efficiency contribution with quantified evidence: Table 1 shows the method needs no per-scene optimization, ~3MB CLIP feature storage versus ~3GB for training-based pipelines, and ~8GB peak VRAM versus ~20-28GB, which is a real practical advantage over the training-based 3DGS open-vocabulary methods it targets.

Competitive/SOTA accuracy on the two reported benchmarks: LERF open-vocabulary object selection reaches 54.3 mean mIoU (vs. LangSplat 51.4, GOI 50.6) and ScanNet segmentation reaches 45.5/47.2/53.7 mIoU over 19/15/10 classes, outperforming the point-based baselines (e.g., Dr.Splat 43.6 mean on LERF) by clear margins.

The ablation in Table 5 gives direct evidence for the cross-view inconsistency argument that motivates the design: VLM-text matching (54.3) substantially beats single-view image matching (36.9), averaged image features (39.2), and filtered image matching (50.1).

The pipeline is simple, modular, and easy to build upon (SAM masks -> DAM2SAM tracking -> back-projection grouping -> neutral-point filtering -> VLM text distillation), and the VLM-agnostic design choice is sensible in principle.
The related-work section covers both the pixel-based and point-based 3DGS open-vocabulary paradigms and clearly states where the authors position their approach.
weaknesses: The headline claim of polysemy is never evaluated. The title, abstract, and introduction build the contribution around polysemous, multi-concept semantics ("a desk point is simultaneously desk, wooden, and furniture"), but no experiment, metric, or qualitative result targets polysemous queries or multi-label assignment; all reported benchmarks (LERF object selection, ScanNet class segmentation) are single-label retrieval/segmentation. Worse, the method itself hard-assigns each Gaussian to exactly one object group (F = {G_j | W1(G_j) > W0(G_j)}), so point-level polysemy is not actually implemented; the only multi-concept behavior is a set of VLM-generated candidate names attached per object, which is a different and much weaker claim than the one advertised.

The most novel module is barely effective by the authors' own ablation. Table 4 shows entropy-based neutral point filtering alone moves mIoU from 53.0 to 53.2 (+0.2), with essentially all of the improvement coming from the opacity filter (53.2 -> 54.3). The thresholds tau_h and tau_alpha are fixed with no sensitivity analysis, so the contribution of the "neutral point processing" claim is weakly supported.

Key baselines and framing are missing or unfair. The paper asserts that existing 3DGS open-vocabulary methods require per-scene training, yet it cites but does not compare against Lu et al. 2025 ("Segment then Splat: A unified approach for 3D open-vocabulary segmentation based on Gaussian splatting") and GradiSeg, which appear to be the most comparable lightweight/training-free competitors. Without these, the claim of outperforming established frameworks is not established. The LERF SOTA claim also rests heavily on one scene: the method loses to LangSplat on ramen (45.6 vs 51.2), teatime (64.4 vs 65.1), and waldo_kitchen (40.9 vs 44.5), with the mean driven by figurines (66.4 vs 44.7).

Reproducibility gaps. The VLM prompt is described only as "a predefined text prompt"; the number of candidate names, their formatting/deduplication, the top-N views, the matching threshold eta, and the fixed values of tau_h and tau_alpha are not reported. The pipeline depends on a proprietary model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) whose call count, latency, and cost are unquantified, and the "VLM-agnostic" claim is asserted with no experiment substituting another VLM. No wall-clock runtime for the pipeline is reported despite the abstract's "hours to minutes" claim; Table 1's "Train Time: None" only says no training occurs. The efficiency comparison also excludes the cost of SAM, DAM2SAM, and VLM inference, which may overstate the practical savings.

Internal inconsistencies and imprecision. The abstract claims a "foreground probability" per Gaussian, but Eq. (3) plus the hard assignment yields a binary foreground/background decision, not a probability. Figure 4's caption discusses InstanceGaussian, which does not appear in the figure (columns are OpenGaussian, Dr.Splat, Ours). Section 3.1 states the pipeline is run independently at three granularity levels to produce a "hierarchical set of masks," but it is never explained how the multi-granularity masks are reconciled in grouping or feature extraction, and granularity is not ablated.

Evaluation breadth is narrow relative to the stated motivation. The introduction motivates autonomous driving and robotics, yet experiments are limited to LERF (4 scenes shown) and ScanNet. No outdoor/large-scale benchmark (e.g., nuScenes, ScanNet++, Replica) is used, and the sensitivity of the method to 3DGS reconstruction quality and sparse views, which the authors themselves list as a limitation, is not quantified.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem statement: the paper diagnoses three concrete limitations of the dominant embedding paradigm (geometry–semantic inconsistency at boundaries, semantic bloat from per-Gaussian feature storage, and semantic rigidity under polysemy) and proposes a coherent alternative rather than a marginal architectural tweak.

The extrinsic, training-free formulation is practically attractive: no per-scene optimization, no gradient-based semantic training, and large reductions in CLIP feature storage (~3MB vs ~3GB) and peak VRAM (~8GB) with an end-to-end runtime of ~9 minutes per scene, as detailed in Tables 1 and 9.

Competitive empirical results on 3D open-vocabulary tasks: best mIoU among 3D methods on ScanNet (45.5/47.2/53.7 for 19/15/10 classes) and best mAcc across all class splits, with consistent qualitative improvements in boundary sharpness over OpenGaussian and Dr.Splat (Figs. 3, 4).

Design choices are supported by ablations: VLM-based text distillation beats CLIP image features (54.3 vs 50.1, Table 5), and the two-stage neutral-point filtering (entropy + opacity) improves over initial grouping (54.3 vs 53.0, Table 4). The supplementary material provides sensitivity analyses on thresholds, VLM choice, prompt count, sparse masks, and failure cases.

Good clarity and reproducibility of internal details: thresholds (τ_h=0.9, τ_α=0.1, η=0.9), the exact VLM prompt template, the object-tracking/detection logic, and per-component runtime breakdowns are documented in the supplement.
weaknesses: Novelty of the 'extrinsic paradigm' is overstated. Prior works such as GS-Grouping (identity encoding), GOI (optimizable semantic hyperplane), Segment-then-Splat, and Occam's LGS already partially decouple semantics from Gaussian geometry through object-level grouping or compact identity codes. The specific realization (VLM text hypotheses + neutral points) is new, but the paradigm framing overstates the conceptual distance from existing work.

The SOTA claim is overreaching. Table 2 shows 2D methods LAGA (64.0) and 3DVLSG (62.0) clearly outperform Ours (54.3) on LERF; the '3.9 mIoU' improvement is only relative to 3D training-free methods. The abstract and main text should explicitly restrict the claim to 3D methods rather than implying overall SOTA.

The efficiency comparison in Table 1 is potentially misleading. Marking 'Scene Opt.: None' and 'Train Time: None' omits the VLM inference cost (37.7% of total runtime per Table 9), mask acquisition (29.7%), and the pre-existing 3DGS optimization the method depends on. The '~3MB' storage number compares only CLIP text features and not the full scene representation, while baselines' numbers include 3DGS optimization.

Heavy dependence on external proprietary models. Table 6 shows a ~7 mIoU swing based on the VLM (SenseNova 6.5 Pro 47.0, InternVL3-78B 50.2, Gemini 2.5 Pro 54.3), so a large fraction of the reported performance derives from a closed API model, raising reproducibility and longevity concerns and limiting the method's standalone technical contribution.

Baseline comparability is questionable. The reported OpenGaussian LERF mIoU (38.4) is far below numbers reported in the original OpenGaussian paper under its own 2D protocol, yet the paper states it follows OpenGaussian's protocol. The manuscript does not clarify whether baseline numbers are copied from original papers, re-implemented, or evaluated under a different protocol, which undermines the fairness of the central comparison.

The claimed polysemy capability (multi-granularity overlapping object grouping) is argued conceptually but never quantitatively evaluated; no metric isolates whether a single Gaussian being assigned to multiple semantic groups actually improves retrieval for ambiguous queries.

Evaluation breadth is limited to LERF and ScanNet, with LERF judged under a non-standard 2D-IoU protocol on manually annotated ground truth. This restricts comparability and leaves generalization to larger, more diverse open-vocabulary benchmarks unverified.

strengths: Introduces a novel extrinsic paradigm that decouples 3D geometry from semantics by storing lightweight textual indices instead of embedding high-dimensional features into Gaussians, directly addressing geometry-semantic inconsistency, semantic bloat, and semantic rigidity.

Achieves substantial efficiency gains: no per-scene semantic optimization, CLIP feature storage reduced from gigabytes to megabytes (~3MB vs ~3GB), and lower peak VRAM (~8GB vs ~20+GB) while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Extensive experiments on LERF and ScanNet, including ablations on neutral point processing, VLM choice, prompt count, feature extraction, sparse mask supervision, and threshold sensitivity, support the design choices.

Qualitative results show sharper object boundaries and better fine-grained selection than OpenGaussian and Dr.Splat, and the supplementary material includes real-world and Grasp-Net evaluations, demonstrating generalization.

The multi-granularity overlapping object grouping enables a single Gaussian to belong to multiple semantic groups, natively supporting polysemy, and the neutral-point handling improves boundary accuracy.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear figures and sufficient implementation details to understand the pipeline.
weaknesses: The SOTA claim is overbroad: Table 2 shows LAGA (64.0 mIoU) and 2D methods such as 3DVLSG (62.0) and Occam's LGS (61.3) outperform the proposed 54.3 mIoU; the 'outperforming previous best by 3.9 mIoU' claim is only valid against the 3D training-free baseline LUDVIG (50.4) and should be explicitly qualified.

The method relies on external pretrained models (SAM, DAM2SAM, and a VLM such as Gemini 2.5 Pro), so errors in masks or VLM-generated nouns propagate; VLM inference alone takes ~9.25 minutes on a Tesla V100 for one complex scene, which limits practicality and reproducibility.

Semantic representation is limited to VLM-generated noun hypotheses encoded by CLIP; complex open-vocabulary queries involving attributes, relations, or rare categories are not systematically evaluated, and the fixed similarity threshold (eta=0.9) is not ablated in the main paper.

The neutral-point thresholds (tau_h=0.9, tau_alpha=0.1) are fixed, and the reported gains are modest (53.0 to 54.3 mIoU); no statistical significance or error bars are provided, making the robustness of the improvement unclear.

The efficiency comparison in Table 1 does not account for base 3DGS reconstruction and data-preparation costs (SAM/DAM2SAM, VLM inference), so 'training-free' refers to semantic adaptation rather than the full pipeline; this should be clarified.

Reproducibility is partially constrained by API-dependent components (Gemini 2.5 Pro, unspecified CLIP variant), and the paper does not mention code release; exact prompt formatting and VLM version may affect results.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated framing of the embedding paradigm's three problems (geometry–semantic inconsistency, semantic bloat, semantic rigidity), and a conceptually clean decoupled 'extrinsic' design in which semantics live in an index layer over object groups rather than in per-Gaussian feature vectors.

The efficiency argument, if accurate, is a genuinely useful contribution: no per-scene semantic optimization, CLIP-feature storage reduced from ~3 GB to ~3 MB, and peak VRAM of ~8 GB versus 20–28 GB for feature-embedding baselines (Table 1). For practitioners this is a meaningful practical property.

Consistent quantitative gains on ScanNet open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation across all three class splits (Table 3: 45.5/47.2/53.7 mIoU vs. 40.7/42.5/47.9 for the strongest baseline, InstanceGaussian), which is the most convincing evidence in the paper.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough: VLM-choice ablation, prompt-count sensitivity, threshold sensitivity for neutral-point filtering, sparse-mask robustness (down to 1/32 of views), failure-case analysis, and object-editing demos. This level of transparency is commendable.

Interesting analytical observations that are not merely rhetorical, e.g., the visualization of viewpoint-dependent CLIP feature inconsistency (Fig. 14) and the statistics showing ~25% of visible Gaussians carry multiple semantic categories (Fig. 13). These support the authors' critique of the embedding paradigm even if they do not validate the proposed fix.
The framework is VLM-agnostic in principle (Table 6 ablates three VLMs), which makes the approach extensible as stronger VLMs appear.
weaknesses: The headline SOTA claim is contradicted by the authors' own table. On LERF (Table 2), LAGA reaches 64.0 mean mIoU and 3DVLGS reaches 62.0, both far above the reported 54.3 for this method. The stated 'outperforming the previous best-performing method by 3.9 mIoU' is obtained only by comparing against LUDVIG (50.4), i.e., within a self-defined '3D training-free' bucket. The paper never justifies excluding LAGA/3DVLGS from the SOTA claim, and this materially overstates the result.

Novelty is thinner than the framing suggests. The pipeline is SAM + DAM2SAM tracking + VLM noun generation + CLIP text encoding + cosine matching, i.e., mostly composition of off-the-shelf components. Object-level (rather than point-level) semantic grouping already exists in GS-Grouping, OpenGaussian instance features, and Segment-then-Splat. The 'neutral point' concept substantially overlaps with boundary/transitional-point work the authors themselves cite ([15], [34]); claiming to 'define the concept' is overstated, and the entropy-plus-opacity filter is a standard two-stage heuristic.

The paper's central claimed advantage over embedding methods — multi-granularity overlapping groups that natively support polysemy — is never ablated. There is no experiment showing that allowing one Gaussian to belong to several groups, or using three granularity levels instead of one, improves any metric. Given that this is listed as contribution #2, the omission is significant.

The efficiency comparison is not apples-to-apples. Table 1 compares raw CLIP feature storage against baselines (LangSplat, Feature-3DGS, Dr.Splat) that explicitly compress features with autoencoders or codebooks, so the '~3 GB' figures are questionable. The accounting also omits SAM/DAM2SAM/VLM inference costs, and 'Scene Opt.: None' glosses over the fact that the method consumes an already-optimized 3DGS scene plus image sequence as input.

Heavy dependence on a proprietary, closed-source VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) that dominates runtime (37.7% of the 555 s/scene budget, Table 9) and is not reproducible or cost-stable. Table 6 shows the VLM choice alone swings mIoU from 47.0 to 54.3, so a large part of the reported performance is attributable to the strength of an external model rather than to the proposed architecture.

Evaluation breadth is limited: LERF (with 2D-proxy IoU and no 3D ground truth) and only 10 ScanNet scenes. No 3D-OVS, Replica, or ScanNet++ evaluation. On LERF the margin over Segment-then-Splat is 2.3 mIoU, and several 2D-method baselines listed in the same table remain substantially better.

Ablation gains are small and internally inconsistent. In Table 4, adding the opacity filter alone degrades mIoU (53.0 → 52.6), and the full model gains only +1.3 over the plain initial grouping; no per-scene variance or significance is reported, so it is unclear whether these differences are meaningful. Similarly, the neutral-point module accounts for 0.1% of runtime, which weakens the case that it is a substantive contribution.

Reporting inconsistency between the main text and the supplementary: the main paper states that the 'top-N masked views with the largest visible areas' are fed to the VLM, whereas the supplementary describes three images in which the target object is highlighted with a green bounding box. The bounding-box hint is a strong localization prior; it is neither ablated nor reconciled with the main-text description, and it plausibly inflates the reported VLM accuracy.

Because semantics are attached to whole object groups, the method cannot answer part-level or attribute-level queries finer than the SAM mask granularity. This sits awkwardly with the paper's motivation around 'rich polysemy', which is discussed qualitatively but never measured, and it limits the claimed generality of the extrinsic paradigm.

Several claims are stated without quantification ('orders of magnitude', 'hours to minutes', 'lightweight', 'robust'). The per-scene runtime of ~9.25 minutes on a V100 (Table 9) is not trivial, and no cost or latency analysis for the VLM API calls is provided.
